So that those who read the record will know what you and I were talking about, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that rule No. 4 to which I referred calls for bills to be accompanied by explanatory notes opposite each clause of the bill. The bill before us has no such explanatory notes on any of the right-hand pages explaining any of the clauses of this bill.
The other aspect of this bill, as to its form, which I submit makes it impossible for us to proceed with it at this time, is that in the bill there is a reference to an agreement; yet the bill does not contain as a schedule thereto the agreement referred to in the bill.
I point out for Your Honour's consideration that the wording in this bill is quite different from that in some other bills in which it is said that the government may enter into an agreement. Rather, the wording here implies the existence of an agreement. I remind Your Honour that there are any number of statutes on our books, such as the Canada Shipping Act; the Great Lakes Fisheries Convention Act; the Bretton Woods Agreements Act; the Terms of Union with Newfoundland (Approval) Act, and a number of others I have listed, such as acts regarding income tax agreements with certain countries, in which parliament was called upon to deal with agreements that had been made by the government with another body or another jurisdiction. In each of those cases the agreement that had been made was made a schedule to the act so that parliament was brought into the picture.
In this case, though the agreement has been tabled and is known as sessional paper No. 174-P of the House of Commons, and though there has been plenty of reference to an agreement, and though some of us have copies of it and know what is in it, this agreement is not made a schedule to the bill. The bill makes reference to some of the conditions that would have to obtain in an agreement between the government and Trans-Canada, but the conditions set out in the bill that that agreement would have to meet are very few. I want to stick directly to the point of order, but just as an example may I point out that there is nothing in the bill that says the agreement must have in it a date by which the western leg of the pipe line is to be completed; there is nothing in the bill which says that the agreement must have in it a date by which the shortterm loan is to be repaid.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.

Because, Mr. Speaker, it is a well established principle of our parliamentary institutions that parliament, indeed the House of Commons in particular, has complete control over the expenditure of money. If we are going to be asked to consider a bill which gives the government the power to make an agreement, the terms of which are not included in the bill, we are thereby giving the government power that properly belongs to the House of Commons.
In that connection, I remind Your Honour of some very important quotations that have been read to this house before by none other than the late William Lyon Mackenzie King. May I refer you in particular to page 159, volume 3 of Redlich, one of the authorities with which Your Honour is quite familiar. He says this:
At first glance there does not appear to be much to learn from tracing the history of the forms of financial procedure. The motive power in financial development is not to be found in procedure, but in the growth of constitutional principles, in the acquisition by parliament of the sole right to grant taxes and in the further evolution of the predominance of the commons as the true representatives of the nation.
Later on the same page he says, and I ask that you take particular note of these words:
Soon after the great change made at the end of the 17th century, political experience showed that a second principle must be established before the foundations of parliamentary government could be regarded as secure. It was necessary to gain for the commons full and unrestricted control over the destination of the money spent, to enable parliament to check its application and to see that expenditure corresponded to the grants made.
Similarly Mr. King on one occasion made reference to Durell's volume entitled, "Parliamentary Grants". In fact I note that certain passages on page 3 of this volume are marked with a pencil and for all I know they may be Mr. King's pencil marks.
It is one of the old standing principles of our constitution that the House of Commons should control the finances of the country. In other words, the cardinal principle on which the whole of our financial system is based is that of parliamentary control, and by this is understood not the control of parliament in its constitutional sense as composed of sovereign, lords, and commons, but control by the commons alone.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.

In other words, after the passing of this bill the government can amend that agreement or make some other kind of agreement which would not have to provide for the repayment of the money or that the company be regarded as in default in the event of failure to achieve construction by a certain date. Therefore, because the agreement is not annexed to this bill as a schedule, because parliament is not made a party to this agreement, we cannot be sure that it will not be altered, amended or substituted, as has already happened in relation to this company.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to part with our control over the ultimate destination of this money; we are being asked to part with control over the guarantee of repayment; we are being asked to part with control over the terms and conditions under which the company would be regarded as succeeding or defaulting. And it is because we are being asked to part with that control that I submit that by this bill in its imperfect form we are being called upon to violate some of these basic principles to which I have already referred.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that though the bill itself does provide certain conditions that must obtain in the agreement, those conditions are far less than are contained in the existing agreement that is circulating amongst us; but we as a parliament are not a party to the agreement circulating amongst us and we will not be a party to it unless it is included in the bill as a schedule thereto.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in view of all the changes, the extensions and so on that have happened in the past, we have the right to feel that unless parliament itself is involved in this agreement, unless we are a party to it, unless it is in the bill, we have no guarantee that the agreement will not be changed by the two parties to it, and I feel that under the basic principle of the right of parliament to maintain control over the voting of money, over the destination of that money, we have the right to have before us a bill which is more than something pretty close to a blank cheque; we have the right to have before us a bill which includes in it as a schedule something that we vote on or in other words the very agreement that is going to be implemented so far as this whole proposition is concerned.
I am not denying the bona fides of the parties that made the agreement that is before us as sessional paper 174-P. The important point is, so long as it is only a two-party agreement those two parties can change it. What we need, if parliament is to be asked to vote for this, is a three-party arrangement. We have to be in on it, too. I submit 

that for reference to be made to this agreement, for it to be tabled, for it to be discussed by the minister who is sponsoring the bill and yet to keep it apart from the bill so that the government and Trans-Canada can amend it or change it as they wish to is being unfair to parliament and to that extent I suggest this bill is imperfect in its form; that it violates the basic principles of parliamentary control over the expenditure of money and that Your Honour should not allow the minister to proceed with it at this time. Indeed, under the provisions of citation 634 of Beauchesne's third edition, I suggest it is quite clear what Your Honour should do. Citation 634 reads:
If the Speaker finds that the bill is in blank or in an imperfect shape, he will decline to put the question and will return the bill to the member who must take another opportunity of bringing it up in conformity with the rules.
Because of the extent to which this bill is blank in that it does not have the agreement attached to it as a schedule, and because of the imperfection in that it violates the principle of parliamentary control over expenditure, I submit that Your Honour should return the bill to the hon. member who is seeking to move it and ask him to correct these imperfections.

The hon. member should perhaps remember that when the motion is made for first reading, the motion in fact has become so purely formal that we do not ask that the bill be now read a first time and be printed but in fact that is being ordered by the house to satisfy the requirements of standing order 74 which says:
All bills shall be printed before the second reading in the English and French languages.

Standing order 72 applies to the introduction and prior to first reading. It says:
No bill may be introduced either in blank or in an imperfect shape.
Therefore at that moment the hon. member cannot raise that point of order because he does not have a copy of the bill. The bill has not been printed. It is my duty, however, to satisfy myself. My satisfaction must be made on a very summary basis because hon. members cannot expect the Speaker to study every bill in an effort to find out whether or not something has been omitted. Hon. members have taken care of that situation themselves by insisting in their procedure that after second reading all bills be referred or committed either to one of their standing committees or to the committee of the whole and even if a bill goes to a standing committee it must be committed to the committee of the whole.
In the committee of the whole proper amendments may be moved, new clauses may be inserted and schedules may be inserted and that is the manner in which it is being done. To raise a point of order and say the second reading of this bill cannot be put because there is an omission in it is not correct. I think the hon. member will admit his point as to explanatory notes is not a good one and I do not think he would insist on that point.

The way the crown signifies its recommendation is through the Speaker now announcing that a royal recommendation has been given to a resolution that outlines the expenditures involved. When we are not dealing with a money bill, the case does not obtain. In this instance we are dealing with a money bill. The

We have examined the resolution, which does not contain any details of the various sections of the bill but just gives an outline of the exependitures contemplated later in the bill. At this moment the bill has received its first reading, and it was ordered to be printed. Now it is up for second reading. If the hon. member's point was right, a new resolution would have to be introduced, because that is the only way to correct something missing in a bill in which the financial initiative of the Crown is involved. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken on the matter referred to in the bill on two earlier occasions and on those occasions I have discussed the subject matter of the bill. On this occasion I should like to
4024	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation speak first about the nature of the project of which this is a part. The project is far larger than the building of a pipe line from the Alberta-Saskatchewan border down to the vicinity of Montreal. The cost of the pipe line itself with its appurtenances is some $375 million which is of course a sizeable amount. But incidental to the building of the pipe line and the operation of the pipe line, a much larger expenditure is involved. It approximates $1 billion. The pipe line itself, of course, is not usable unless branch distribution systems are provided in the cities and towns along the way.
A great number of these cities and towns have already taken out franchises for gas distribution within the community and are only waiting to have the supply of gas definitely fixed before proceeding with their local development. In the province of Alberta a great number of gas wells must be drilled to make deliverable the gas that has been proven there, and also chemical plants must be built to remove the sulphur, butane and other liquids to make the gas suitable for the pipe line. It is a project that should appeal, I think, to the Canadian people, a project extending across five provinces and a project which means the replacement of great quantities of fuel presently imported from the United States with lower cost fuel produced within Canada.
The production of gas in Alberta goes back a good many years. I lived in Alberta for quite a period more than 40 years ago. The house which I occupied was equipped to use natural gas for heating and all other purposes. At that time gas had been brought into Calgary from the vicinity of Medicine Hat and the cost of heating in Calgary had been greatly reduced as a result of that service. Later on gas was brought into the city of Edmonton by a group headed by Mr. Ray Milner, whom I knew very well in Dalhousie. I was on the staff and he was a student. He was able to get financial help from the United States and, over the years, has built up a distribution system within the city of Edmonton.
However, the major discoveries of gas have occurred in recent years as part of the development of the petroleum industry. The natural resources of Alberta, of course, belong to the province, but licences have been issued to private industry to develop certain areas and the gas that has been developed and proven up is the property of those licensees of the Alberta government. Who are the principal holders of gas in that province? The largest is Canadian Gulf. Canadian Gulf is the owner of about one-third of all the proven gas supplies. The


second largest holder is the Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company, which is working in co-operation with the Hudson's Bay Company in developing the mineral rights that are controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company. The third largest is the Standard Oil of California and the fourth largest is the Canadian Delhi Company.
It is interesting to note that the largest holder of gas in Alberta, the second largest holder of gas in Alberta and the fourth largest holder of gas in Alberta are the principal sponsors of the project that we are discussing today. It has been suggested in this house that these men who control Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited have been offering gas for export at less than the most favourable prices available. It seems rather extraordinary to me, and I think it will seem extraordinary to every hon. member in this house, if these companies have been offering gas, which they own, for export at a price lower than that obtainable from other sources.
These men have become interested in the pipe line so that they may obtain an outlet for the gas they own and for other gas available within Alberta. This has been the reason for their sponsorship of the project. The group that is sponsoring the program have bought shares to a value in excess of $15 million, and bought them for cash. They bought them at a price of $8 per share. This is one project in Canada in which there is not a single share that has not been bought at $8 or, if bought recently, $8 plus interest from the time the group was formed.
These men have been undertaking the work that is necessary before a project of this kind can move. They have been making the surveys of potential markets. They have retained consulting engineers who have prepared the engineering for the project. Earlier the group provided funds to build a gas line from the Niagara river to Toronto in order that a start could be made upon conversion to natural gas in the Toronto area and in order to develop additional markets there. They have acquired rights of way, and particularly the right of way across western Canada from Calgary to the Manitoba border. They have been working for the greater part of two years doing the necessary preliminary work for the building of the pipe line which we are discussing today. What has the government done to help? Absolutely nothing in a financial way. Not one cent of government money has played any part in the development up to the present time. What is the government's interest in the project?
Well, it seems to me a very definite interest in the project arises out of the government

policy affecting energy produced in Canada. This policy was announced some five years ago in the House of Commons, and was that the policy in connection with natural gas would be parallel with the policy on energy in the form of electricity, namely that energy in the form of gas must be made available to Canadian consumers and that only quantities of gas that are clearly in excess of the present or future needs of Canadian consumers could be permitted to move outside Canada. Having announced that policy the government, in my opinion, has some responsibility for seeing that the means of moving gas to markets available in Canada should be provided. Certainly, we had an interest in that project and we have taken an interest, not a financial interest but we have moved to the extent that we could to encourage the planning of this pipe line.
Early in the history of this scheme a proposal was made, not by the present group but by another-the hon. member for Calgary South will remember-that instead of moving gas from Alberta to these markets by a pipe line, we should allow gas to be exported south from Calgary and recovered in the vicinity of Toronto on an exchange basis. The government was unable to consider that proposal. Then a proposal was received that instead of an all-Canadian pipe line the sponsors be permitted to follow the route of the oil pipe line from Alberta; that is, a route down through the United States. There again the government rejected that proposal and said that gas must be brought to eastern Canada by an all-Canadian pipe line. That position was rather resented in Alberta. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle) has spoken about it in the House of Commons. It is claimed that we are putting an improper tax on the owners of the gas and making the project of supplying that gas to Canadians in eastern Canada uneconomical.
I went to Calgary at the invitation of the petroleum institute and addressed its members there at a dinner meeting. I was warned beforehand that I must submit myself to questioning after the meeting was over. I went there for the purpose of explaining why it is in the national interest that eastern Canada be served with Alberta natural gas through an all-Canadian pipe line. I had the honour of having my friend, the hon. member for Calgary South, sit beside me on that occasion. Whether I was able to convince him that evening, or whether he has seen the light since, I am not sure. But I think perhaps at some stage we have made progress in a meeting of minds on the proper method for distributing western 67509-255i
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation Canadian gas. I explained the need for an all-Canadian line. I admitted that it would be more costly than alternative plans, but I said the added cost is one of the penalties we must accept for Canadian nationhood. I remember my words. I said: "There is a price on Canadian nationhood. If we always looked for the cheapest way of doing things here in Canada there might have been another state in the United States but there very likely would have been no Canada. From confederation the people of Canada have been very jealous about accepting any monetary advantage that would in any way jeopardize the control by Canada over her own resources."
It was that line that I pursued in my discussion before the petroleum institute. I must say that that position seemed to be accepted by the industry that was gathered there on that occasion; for, following the meeting, there did not seem to be any subject about which they wished to question me; at least, no questions were asked. Since then the government's requirement for an allCanadian pipe line has been accepted as a national necessity by the industry.
Then, naturally, I have followed the efforts of the sponsors of the pipe line to finance their project. I have discussed the problems with the sponsors themselves, with their bankers and with others who have attempted to assist in carrying out the project. I may say that Premier Frost over several years has been just as interested as I have been to bring about the delivery of gas into his province, and on two or three occasions I have met him, together with representatives of the pipe line company, in an effort to assist the project.
A study of the financial situation indicated that to finance the whole line across Canada, the type of line that we feel is needed for the purpose, would not be possible unless some means could be found to bridge the first three, four or five years of build-up in eastern Canada. Eastern Canada, which has never used natural gas, which in the main had no facilities for using it, presented a problem where time would probably be required before we had a financeable project to place before the banks. Well, how could the government assist in that situation? It was found that by removing the financing of the northern Ontario section, as covered by a section in the bill before us, the remainder could be financed from the inception, and given three, four or five years, the project would be in an earning position that would enable it to buy the government section. An arrangement was worked out by which the government could not possibly fail to recover
4026	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation its investment over a period, which would provide for the building by the government and the use by the company of the northern Ontario section, which would result in an easing of the financial burden in the early years to be recouped when the earning period began. That provision is contained in the bill.
The government of Ontario indicated not only an interest but a real financial interest in that section of the work. It is estimated to cost $118 million. The proposal was that the province of Ontario would share one-third of the cost up to $35 million and that the federal government would provide the remainder of the money required to build the section of the line from the Manitoba border to Kapuskasing. Then the company undertook to finance the line. Part of the revenue on which we had been counting at all stages was revenue derived from the export of 200 million cubic feet of gas which was found to be in excess of present and future Canadian requirements. The company dealt with interested parties in that connection. They first had a contract for a smaller amount with the Northern Natural Gas Company which supplies the Minneapolis and northern Wisconsin area. That contract called for a rate of 29 cents, which was satisfactory to the sponsors of Trans-Canada.
Northern Natural made an application to the federal power commission and immediately ran into a storm of protests from their customers in the area, on the grounds that the offered price was too high and that the offer would involve higher rates to the present customers of Northern Natural Gas. The protests of the customers were effective with the federal power commission and the result was that the hearing on that application adjourned sine die. The contract with Natural Gas had a clause permitting either side to cancel unless the contract was implemented within a certain short period, I think it was one year. The time had elapsed. The Trans-Canada sponsors were unable to obtain a renewal of the contract. It was said that a lower price would be required, but Northern Natural have never named that lower price that they would require, and since no progress could be made with Northern Natural, Trans-Canada, to leave itself free to deal with others, cancelled the contract under the terms thereof. Then we had representations from a group including Northern Natural, People's Gas and American Pipelines Company. It was represented that this group would be able to make a proposal that would be attractive for the export of gas. The group met with me. I told them I had nothing to do with making a contract for the gas, that 

they should prepare their proposal and submit it to the sponsors of the Trans-Canada company. Later on I received a letter from them in general terms. I wrote back and said I hoped they would be successful in reaching an agreement with Trans-Canada.

That letter has been tabled, incidentally. Mr. Merriam of the group went to Calgary and met with the sponsors of Trans-Canada. It was reported to me that he had no firm proposal to make. Shortly after that a proposal was received from Tennessee Gas Transmission. That proposal was a firm proposal. It had several advantages other than the sale of gas. True, the price was lower than in the contract it superseded. The price was 25J cents per thousand cubic feet. The load factor was 95 per cent and the proposal contained an escalation clause which provided for an increasing price year by year during the term of the contract, which proposals by the other group did not contain.
In any event the sponsors decided the Tennessee proposal to be the most favourable received and a contract was signed with that company. Application was made before the federal power commission by Tennessee to implement the contract and the hearing on that application has been proceeding now for some seven or eight months.
The application has probably met with the most violent opposition in the history of the federal power commission. The results of the hearing are still unknown and that fact has seriously interfered with the financing of the pipe line. Had the application been approved, the line would have been financed and under way long before this.
Hon. members complain that we have been late in bringing down this bill. The reason we have been late is that we were hoping a compromise would be arrived at which would permit an early decision by the F.P.C. In that we were disappointed. We also hoped that temporary financing could be arranged which would make government assistance in the western section unnecessary. In that we were disappointed. After we decided that direct government action was necessary if we were to get a program under way this year it took some time to work out the details of the program as represented by the

bill before you and the agreement that has been tabled with the bill. So much for the position today.
The question has been asked: "Who was pressing for action?" Well, I think I can throw some light on that subject. We have received several letters. The letters I will read have all been tabled and are available to hon. members.
The first letter I will read is dated April 24, 1956, from Premier Manning of Alberta, addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent):
My dear Prime Minister:
Passing through Ottawa today, I had hoped to have an opportunity to discuss with you the serious situation developing as a result of the prolonged delay in getting the trans-Canada pipe line project under way. This was not possible due to your engagement in Toronto, and as previous commitments prevent me staying over until tomorrow, I had a brief discussion with your colleague, the Right Hon. Mr. Howe, and am writing this letter to outline some of the thoughts I had hoped to discuss with you personally.
My colleagues and I have become increasingly concerned over the serious threat to the whole national gas development and gas utilization program occasioned by the repeated frustrations and delays that have attended the proposed trans-Canada pipe line project. For the following reasons, in our opinion the situation has reached the point where any further delay in commencing at least the western section of the line may well prove disastrous to the entire project.

It will be extremely difficult to grant further indefinite extensions of the government permits, and almost impossible for the company to retain existing contracts with gas producers.
2.	Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and the Alberta Trunk Line Company have made arrangements for the large dimension pipe necessary for the project if it proceeds this year. If it is delayed another year this pipe, in all probability, will be allocated to some other project. If this happens it will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the company to make firm arrangements for the delivery of the necessary pipe in time to commence construction in 1957.
3.	Another year's delay in providing a market for Alberta gas will have a retarding effect on the development of both the oil and gas resources of the province. Millions of dollars of investment capital already are immobilized in gas wells which are capped because no export market is available. A program involving over $100 million of new development for gathering lines, processing plants and auxiliary industries which large scale export of gas will make possible is being held in abeyance, and each further delay is undermining confidence in the future prospects to a degree that is damaging to both the provincial and the national interests.
4.	Public acceptance of the present national gas policy which dictates that Canadian consumers be given first priority in the use of Canadian gas
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation is being weakened by the prolonged delay in getting western gas to eastern consumers. A policy impossible of practical application in a reasonable period of time cannot indefinitely command public endorsation and support. Over two years have lapsed since the present trans-Canada project was formulated as a vehicle to implement national policy with respect to natural gas. To date western producers have not been able to sell one cubic foot of gas for delivery to eastern consumers. Living with this situation every day, we are very conscious of the extent to which the uncertainty created by repeated delays is undermining the confidence of investors and producers, and of the public generally.
For these reasons we believe it is of the utmost importance that at least the western section of the proposed line oe constructed this year. In fairness to the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company, I believe it rightly can be said they have complied with every condition and requirement of the national gas policy laid down by your government. They have encountered temporary difficulty in financing their part of the project only because of the delay before the federal power commission at Washington, which is something entirely beyond their control.
Under these circumstances, we feel your government would be fully justified in taking whatever steps are necessary and in your judgment proper to ensure the immediate start of the Trans-Canada project within the framework of the national policy that precludes consideration of other markets until eastern Canada is served.
I respectfully submit these observations for your consideration, with the sincere hope that you will be able to make an early announcement that construction of the line will commence this spring.
Yours very sincerely,
Ernest C. Manning,
Premier of Alberta.

Jear Mr. Howe:
I beg to acknowledge your letter of May 11, in which you outline the present status of the project for trans-Canada gas pipeline, and the financial arrangements recently concluded between your government and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited in order that construction of the western section will commence this year.
As we have frequently stated, a trans-Canada pipeline is, of course, a federal responsibility. A provincial government is in no position, constitutionally, to assume any responsibility for decisions as to the construction or the financing of a national undertaking that crosses the boundaries of several provinces. We have, however, from the outset concurred in the policy of a line that would be built entirely within the boundaries of Canada, within Canadian jurisdiction. As a provincial government we are particularly interested in the potential benefits for northern Ontario that would undoubtedly follow the building of a gas pipeline through that portion of the province. Generally, in view of our rapid industrial expansion, coupled with the fact that our hydro-electric power resources are now approaching their maximum limits of development, the necessity of new sources of fuel for our industries and our domestic consumers is becoming increasingly urgent. We agree with you that further delays in the construction of this project would have very adverse consequences. Time has become of the essence. Every day's delay invites the most serious consequences to the development of Ontario, and to the national economy. In these circumstances, it would appear essential that the western section of the line be completed during the year 1956. To accomplish this, we understand that actual construction must be commenced not later than July 1. We understand from your letter that your financial arrangements with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited are designed to accomplish this purpose.
You will recall that our agreement with your government, as set out in the correspondence of November, 1955, provided for the incorporation of a crown corporation to build the northern Ontario section of the trans-Canada line. The conditions upon which we agreed to lend money to such a corporation, to the limit of $35 million, were as follows:
1.	That our investment would be returned to us out of rentals based upon the through-put of gas, with interest at the going rate, so that eventually this investment would involve no cost to the taxpayers of Ontario.
2.	That we should not be called upon to advance money under commitment until you were able to assure us that all other portions of the entire trans-Canada line from Alberta to Quebec would be completed and operated.
3.	That by reason of the terms of the agreement between your government and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, our commitment would terminate


if the company were unable by May 1, 1956, to show financial ability to carry out their entire undertaking.
In any matter of such complexity and magnitude, we recognize that it may become necessary to consider changes in arrangements from time to time. At the last session of the legislature an act was passed, by the unanimous recorded vote of the house, giving authority to enter into such arrangements. The act allows for certain flexibility so as to meet changing situations as they may arise. Section 1 of the act is as follows:
"1. For the purpose of implementing the arrangements made or to be made between the government of Canada and the government of Ontario to facilitate the construction of a connecting link through northern Ontario of a pipeline to transport natural gas from Alberta into central Ontario, the treasurer of Ontario is hereby authorized to loan from time to time out of the consolidated revenue fund any sum of money, but not more than $35 million, to a corporation constituted or to be constituted on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada and having as a purpose the construction aforesaid."
Upon condition that the construction of the western section begins not later than July 1, 1956. we are willing to concur in the extension of time that you request. Subject to this change, we shall continue our commitment to participate in the financing of the northern Ontario section.
Yours sincerely,
Dana Porter.

What is the record of this company, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited? For five long years we have been waiting for action. Throughout that entire period this company has played a monopoly game without chance. Its attitude has been one of artful juggling. It has changed its front from year to year. From year to year this cobweb of colourful finance has been spun.
They started with the idea that they could finance themselves. They said they needed no government help. They secured an incorporation on that basis, and having designedly made the allegation that under no circumstances would they ask for assistance, they began that tortuous course they have followed ever since. First they said, "We will ship directly to the Ontario and Quebec markets and provide the necessary pipe line." Their next attitude was, "We will change that; we need United States markets and we will build a spur line to the United States boundary and that spur line will supply the great needs of the middle west."
They were able to contact in the United States three companies named by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who were prepared to pay a real price, a price far in excess of what is to be paid today by the

Today the Minister of Trade and Commerce says the reason this was not gone ahead with was that there were complaints from the consumers. Nothing of the kind. That statement is unjustified, for after a lapse of a few months and consideration being given by the federal power commission, suddenly the whole matter was dropped by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
Their next proposition was that they would have to get some assistance in order to bridge northern Ontario. No; I am ahead of myself. As a matter of fact it is difficult to follow this company in the labyrinth of financial manipulation, and one is apt to forget the changes of front that have been made. First they asked for a guarantee of assistance from the industrial development bank, and that was denied. Then they came along with a new proposition, a complete change of front. They said they would need assistance by way of the creation of a crown corporation to bridge that area of northern Ontario which would be unprofitable.
So the changes have gone on. Throughout that entire period, whatever change of front this favoured corporation has made, how often it has altered its course, it has still been able to command the benediction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and today he is joined with the amens of every member of the cabinet. Why? Why does this corporation enjoy such a peculiarly favoured position in the heart of this government? Why are competing corporations given no opportunity even to submit a proposition? Those are questions on which we require information; those are questions on which we have a right to obtain information.
Let us follow the course of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In March, 1953, he said this was economically feasible to build. He was the man who was able to secure the merger of Trans-Canada and Western Pipe Lines. He said, "There is no danger at all; there is no reason for delay. In March of 1953 he said, at page 2929 of Hansard:
The policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipe line across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
A little later on in that speech he said:
This government has reason to believe that it is economically feasible to build a gas pipe line from southern Alberta to Toronto and Montreal, serving the intervening Canadian cities.
And then this master of optimism said this on December 1, 1954: "I believe that the construction of Trans-Canada will begin in 1955; that the building of the pipe line

Why has the government-and I ask the Prime Minister to give an answer on behalf of this government-displayed such solicitude, such a keen feeling of regard for this corporation? Mr. Speaker, we want to break through that wall of secrecy that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has built not only around himself and parliament but around his colleagues in the cabinet. I shall just read a few lines in the letter-there is a long letter of April 4-which starts off in this way:
I appreciated the opportunity of seeing you on March 27 in Ottawa to discuss an alternate proposal to supply Alberta natural gas to eastern Canada. Confirming my representations to you at that time, I am prepared to undertake a Canadian-owned, privately financed project to construct an economically feasible gas pipe line from Alberta to Montreal if Trans-Canada is not immediately able to present a suitable proposal and some plan to break the present deadlock which is preventing the construction of the eastern Canadian pipe line.
What more do you want? "This is my proposal", he says. How else do you submit a proposal before it is actually translated into the formality of a legal document? Then he goes on to say this:
The closest and most logical market for surplus Canadian gas is in the existing pipe-line companies and distributors in the great plains-mid-west area of the United States. The three companies which presently serve this area, the American Natural Gas Company, People's Gas Light and Coke Company, and Northern Natural Gas Company, are prepared to purchase from a truly Canadian pipe line 400,000 mcf per day of gas at Emerson, Manitoba, under a 25-year contract to supplement their own supplies of gas. With this sale an allCanadian pipe line project is economically feasible on a sound business basis without government financing or debt guarantee.
Had not McMahon proven that before? Had he not proven his capacity? He had already done that in another company.
Then it goes on to say:
With this sale an all-Canadian pipe-line project is economically feasible on a sound business basis without government financing or debt guarantee. These companies want no stock-interest in the Canadian pipe line company and in fact they desire that international dealings be on an arms-length basis.
Then he says:
It is further evident that Trans-Canada is controlled by United States financial interests and that it is influenced and dominated by Tennessee Gas Transmission Company. The plan proposed by Trans-Canada strongly favours Tennessee Gas Transmission Company to the detriment of Canada.
Was it because these letters contained that damning indictment that they were hidden? Is that the reason? After all, McMahon had established his right to know. He says:
I am firmly of the opinion that the Trans-Canada proposal to receive governmental subsidy through the crown corporation "bridge" and to sell gas for underground storage in the United States rather than to use southern Ontario underground storage to the fullest extent is not in the best interests of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when you are asking as to what is in the best interests of Canada, don't you believe that a Canadian could possibly give you as good advice as those from the Tennessee corporation in the United States?
With this in mind, I am enclosing a second memorandum which outlines the basic fault of the Trans-Canada plan.
The Prime Minister was never allowed even a peek at it, yet the cabinet had to decide which was the best. Apparently they had no benefit of any criticism of the plan that was submitted to the cabinet, although the responsible minister had the document in his pocket. It does look strange. It does ask for the opening of the gate just a little bit. It does demand that the searchlight of investigation be permitted to light up these darkened places. Never before has a pocket been such a dark place.

Would the Prime Minister not have given consideration to the McMahon plan if he had known that this company, already established and not dependent upon the illusory possibility of confirmation of plans by the federal power commission, was prepared to pay more than any of .these other companies? Surely, Mr. Speaker, this document that remained ensconced in the bosom of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if it had ever been revealed to the light of day would at least have been an argument to be considered by the cabinet. But no; the Prime Minister honestly told parliament, "I never saw it".
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Now we come to the last part of this momentous document, the memorandum re basic faults of the Trans-Canada plan:
An all-Canadian pipe line can be built from Alberta to eastern Canada on a sound business basis without government financing or debt guarantee provided that the pipe-line company is constituted to further the interests of Canada and sell surplus gas in sufficient volume at an economic price to the existing pipe lines which now serve the great plains-midwest area of the United States.
The right hon. gentleman says that we are anti-American. We are not; we are proCanadian. That is the difference. We think it is pro-Canadian to get the largest possible price from an available market rather than turn over this natural resource to the vagaries of decisions by a foreign board. Sir, Trans-Canada as constituted at the present time is controlled by United States financial interests-this is what this memorandum says-and is dominated by Tennessee Gas Transmission Company, so the principal interest behind Canada's pipe line is dealing with itself as the principal purchaser in the United States. I continue:
Trans-Canada, so influenced and dominated, proposes an uneconomic plan to favour Tennessee Gas to the detriment of Canada and at the same time requests the governments of Canada and Ontario to subsidize the $122 million pipe line "bridge" across northern Ontario in order to make it possible to put the proposal into effect.
Has there ever been an indictment of the plans of any company to equal that, Mr. Speaker? It is detrimental to Canada and detrimental to the producers in Alberta, since the price they will receive will be less because these companies that are to be preferred in the United States, the dominated puppets of Gardiner Symonds, are dealing with themselves. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a remark that the project of the building of a trans-Canada pipe line should be one which should appeal to all the people of Canada, and I want to say that I am in accord with that statement.
There are certain provisos that I would make. First of all, of course, it should be shown that the pipe line would be economically sound from the point of view of Canada.
I believe that can be done. Then, too, there is a vast quantity of gas in the province of Alberta which should not be allowed to go to waste and which should be utilized as speedily as possible. I think all Canadians would agree with that, because while that gas is in the province of Alberta it is indeed a resource that in reality belongs to all the people of Canada and should be utilized for the benefit of Canada.
One of the objections I have to the proposal now before us is that the success of the trans-Canada line from the point of view of the present project and company depends so largely on a decision of the federal power commission of the United States. I do not think that is a very dignified position for the country to be in, and I believe we should consider the alternatives to this plan. In my opinion there is only one alternative, and that alternative is that we shall build and operate the pipe line as a public utility. I do not say that the line should be built by the federal parliament of Canada alone if the provinces wish to co-operate in the building of the line.
If on the other hand a better plan would be to build the pipe line wholly under the jurisdiction of this federal parliament of Canada, then the provinces could take the gas from the line and distribute that gas in their own provinces under their own plans. The provinces that today have power commissions could distribute the gas through their own power commissions. If any one of them wished to distribute through a private enterprise organization, that would be the decision of the province concerned. But to my mind it would be an economically sounder
4046	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation proposition in every respect for the government of Canada, which can raise the finances much more cheaply than can a private company, to undertake this plan and do it by itself.
The bill before us falls into two parts. The first part of the bill deals with the setting up of the crown company. I want to say immediately that when we are undertaking a major project of this description, I think a crown company is the proper way in which to do it, a crown company that can be brought before the appropriate parliamentary committee and questioned on its operations, but that operates independently of day to day interference and control of the House of Commons.
As I have said, the bill falls into two parts. It sets up for the purposes of the act a corporation to be called the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. Then it provides for the officers of that corporation. We know that the corporation will be the agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada. That is all to the good. Then I think the bill is spoiled by saying that this crown corporation is authorized and expected to do certain things for the company to be known as Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, a private corporation which, as has been so often demonstrated already in this debate, is under the financial control of powerful United States gas and oil companies, and the majority control of which is held in the United States.
I recollect over the years the manner in which we have been told from time to time- and I remember statements by Mr. Mackenzie King, of course in another connection, for example in connection with the setting up of the Bank of Canada-that those who controlled the financial affairs of the country in reality controlled the country. Although the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon tried to tell us something different, I am still of the opinion that the real control of any corporation or any organization lies in those who are in control of the finances of the corporation.
So then we have the two parts of this bill. First there is the principle of the bill setting up this crown corporation and giving it certain obligations and certain powers. Then there is part II of the bill which deals with the building of the western section of the pipe line from the Alberta-Saskatchewan border to Winnipeg or a point in the vicinity of Winnipeg; and in the building of that part of the line we have undertaken an obligation, according to the bill, to finance that section to the extent of 90 per cent, not to exceed $80 million, and the company itself-so the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us the


other day-would have an investment of some $15 million initially.
Hence in reality what we are doing is handing over to this new corporation-which as I say is an American corporation-some $80 million to build that part of the pipe line. It may be said, of course, that the company will be obligated to pay 5 per cent interest, but the interest rate is not the real factor. The real factor is the amount of money we are putting into this project, namely $80 million. The bill also provides that the crown corporation shall be able to expend, lend or otherwise dispose of some $130 million altogether.
When you look at these provisions you see what we are doing for this company. While we with the province of Ontario are obligated to build the bridge across northern Ontario and with them are going to appropriate $118 million for that purpose, there is still left the gap between the city of Winnipeg or a point in the vicinity of Winnipeg and the Ontario-Manitoba border. We do not know how that is going to be financed. If the company cannot finance the first leg-which is an easy leg and which should be a productive leg

from the Saskatchewan-Alberta border to Winnipeg, how is it going to finance the more difficult piece of territory from Winnipeg to the Ontario border?
I am not so much interested in an argument as between the companies that were involved in the discussions which led up to the trans-Canada pipe line. For example, I do not think the record of Mr. McMahon, who has been talked about this afternoon, is one which recommends him to the attention of this House of Commons or this parliament. From what we know of his operations in Canada and elsewhere I think there is little to choose between Mr. McMahon and some of the other people whom we at times have referred to as economic buccaneers. I cannot see anything to choose between them. If Canada is going to be skinned, I would just as soon be skinned by an American as by a Canadian financial man.
I therefore do not think it is worth while to enter into a discussion of the relative merits of Mr. McMahon, Mr. Murchison or any of these other gentlemen. However, I want to say this to the government. I cannot understand part II of the bill. I cannot understand why part II of the bill refers to an unidentified agreement. I cannot understand why part II of the bill states:
Pursuant to an agreement in that behalf made, with the approval of the governor in council, before or after the coming into force of this act, between Her Majesty and Trans-Canada . . .
And so on. I cannot understand why this is spoken .of as an agreement. Any agreement that has been made between the government

of Canada and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited should be identified, at the very least. Of course I think my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was perfectly right this afternoon when he argued that the agreement should form an integral part of this bill and be appended to it.
I know there are hon. gentlemen sitting opposite and in the cabinet who have had long experience in public life in this country and two of whom have headed the governments of their respective provinces. I doubt very much whether either of them, in conducting the affairs of their respective provinces at that time, and in making an agreement similar to this with a private company and bringing in a bill, would not have appended the agreement to the bill so the legislature-and as we are now, this parliament-would have the right not only to discuss the agreement but to decide upon it and have a firm understanding of it.
As a matter of fact, when we look into this particular section of the bill what do we find? We find certain deficiencies in it. In this bill no date is named for the completion of the western section that we are financing, and no date is set for the repayment of the loan of some $80 million which we are making. Why are these two important details not included in the bill itself, as well as in the agreement which should be attached to the bill? As a matter of fact I think one could argue from the wording of this section of the bill that the governor in council might have the power to vary this agreement, to enter into an agreement with the other party to extend the time, or to extend the payments, or to do other things which we do not expect will be done and which certainly should not be done without the consent of this parliament. So I say, then, that part II of the bill now before us is deficient.
I would say to the government that when this bill goes into committee I think the government should move to have any agreement which has been signed made an appendix to the act which this bill will become when it is passed. I think that would be wise. speechtext:
Our C.C.F. friends are certainly worrying about the people of Alberta. The people of Alberta have slapped them in the face and kicked them time after time after time, yet they think they must be the little white-winged saviours of the people of
[Mr. Blackmore.!

Alberta, just as if the people of Alberta did not know something about these matters themselves.
In order to give some idea of just how badly Alberta is injured by the private enterprise we have there, which has done so much in the development of our industry and of course has aroused the greenest envy on the part of the C.C.F. people, may I tell the story, as far as I have the opportunity to tell it in the time at my disposal, of one of the gas reservoirs in the province of Alberta. This one is in the riding of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) about 25 miles from where I live, and is near the town of Pincher Creek. It is called the Pincher Creek wet gas field. In order to tell the story properly I should like to lead up to the discovery of the project by telling something about the history of the gas and oil industry in southern Alberta, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce did this afternoon.
From Peace river to the border and from the Rocky mountains to Saskatchewan, Alberta is already dotted with scores of gas fields and single well gas discoveries. For those who have never seen one of these fields, may I try to give some sort of idea of the kind of deposit these fields are in and the kind of job a company has to do in order to discover gas. What is a gas and oil field deposit like? It is like an unopened oyster shell lying on its side and buried in the ground. That is a fairly good picture of what a gas field is as nature left it. There is a large stone-like structure around the oval space and the oil body lies in the bottom of the oval much as soup will lie in the bottom of a soup tureen, lying on the floor of the oval chamber, so to speak. In above the gasoline and oil, between the surface of the gasoline and oil and the ceiling or roof of the rounded stone structure, gas has collected down through the ages; and because of the way in which it collects it comes to exert an enormous pressure on the surface of the oil which lies at the bottom of the oval structure. The gas presses on the oil. As soon as the drill goes down and pierces through the upper shell, we will say of the oyster, and goes down far enough, then the pressure of the gas on the oil surface forces the oil up through the pipe and out where people can get at it.
Now we come particularly to the wet gas field of Pincher Creek. This wet gas field- and I am thinking now in terms of the oyster shell-is seven miles long and about three miles wide at its widest place. The porous Madison limestone reservoir is buried two and a half miles deep-two and a half miles deep is the oyster shell-in the foothills of the Rocky mountains about 15 miles north

of the Canadian and American border between Pincher Creek and Waterton Lakes national park. The ridge containing the reservoir- the ridge itself-lies buried more than one and a half miles below the surface of the great Pacific ocean that rolls its way 500 miles west beyond the Rocky mountains. Just think of the task involved, first of all in finding where that oil deposit lay and second, in getting down to the oil deposit and bringing the oil up.
The pool contains about 2,400 billion cubic feet of raw wet gas-just think how much that is-a mixture of natural gas, gasoline, condensate and light crude oil, sulphur, propane, butane and ethane. The difference between wet gas and dry gas is that wet gas contains all these substances which I have mentioned, while dry gas contains none of them but is practically ready to be used as gas immediately.
The worth of the whole mass of content of this field is more than half a billion dollars. Of this, 2,400 billion cubic feet of raw wet gas, 37j per cent or 1,920 billion cubic feet, worth $211 million itself, would be dry gas. The other 62-| per cent of the value could not be recovered until the 1,920 million cubic feet of dry gas was disposed of, or marketed which means that even after the company gets down and finds the gasoline and finds the gas it is unable to use that gasoline and the contents of the gas until it can sell the dry gas after they remove the other substances from the wet gas.
Now hon. members can see how difficult a position the company is placed in unless it can first of all find a market for the dry gas. They cannot take up any of the contents of that great body of value until they can get a market for the dry gas. But the Conservative and C.C.F. members of this house are doing everything in their power to prevent them from selling their gas so they can take out the sulphur, butane, propane and all the other substances in that gas, and the whole quantity must lie there as an absolutely dead asset.
They are brilliant Canadians, these C.C.F.'ers, and these Conservatives, in trying to block the development of great values of that kind. Their only excuse is that they just do not know what they are doing. If they knew one-fiftieth of what they think they know, they would be brilliant; I think they would all be in universities. Unless and until Alberta and Canada are able to market the dry gas from the Pincher Creek wet gas field there will be in that field frozen assets of Canada-belonging to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland just as much as to Alberta,

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation but equally useless to Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, British Columbia as to Alberta-until the field can be developed. That is what we are struggling about now, to be able to develop the field.
In the field there are the following; sulphur, some 7,400,000 long tons, estimated to be worth $163 million; condensate and light crude oil, 38,400,000 barrels worth $126 million; natural gasoline, some 9,800,000 barrels worth $24,700,000; propane, some 12,700,000 barrels worth $21,300,000-I hope the C.C.F. can understand what dollars mean-butane, some 10,400,000 barrels worth $16,300,000; the total value of these frozen assets being $351,300,000. All of this the noble Conservatives and the equally noble C.C.F.'ers are trying to prevent from being realized. Is it not a brilliant record? Yet they call themselves Canadians, they call themselves intelligent, and they consider themselves to be responsible.
That is the gift which the great Creator prepared for North America in the district between Pincher Creek and Waterton Lakes park. If it had not been for this private enterprise which the C.C.F. seem so much to abhor, that gas would have remained in that field for perhaps another thousand years, because there is only one kind of organization that has the money to make it able to dare risk the cost of discovering a field like that. The only kind of concern that has that money is really a giant, and the only place you find such giants is in the United States.
Let us see who it was that found this great deposit. From the time away back in the 1890's when two old-timers, Lafayette French and Kootenay Brown traded some Indians a horse for a certain slough from the surface of which neighbouring Indians had long been skimming a brown oily liquid with a vile smell and certain useful properties-from those days on-the idea lingered that oil could be found in southwestern Alberta; but it was only the idea. I can remember distinctly how they used to talk about it when I was a small boy.
In 1901-we are now tracing the development of this story up to where we have this wonderful field now all ready to be used- French and Brown showed three Calgary pioneers, namely A. P. Patrick, John Line-ham and George Leeson, their slough and gave them the idea of oil. We were getting a little nearer. The Rocky Mountain Development Company was formed. A forest of tents sprang up around the slough, drilling started, the first Alberta oil boom got under way and suddenly collapsed.
4056	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Why? Largely because there was not a company strong enough to carry on. Between 1901 and 1920 at least a dozen wells were drilled in the Cameron brook area- Cameron brook is a brook in the Water ton Lakes park not far from this field-near where Lafayette and Kootenay got their idea. Through the years within a 25-mile radius of the present Pincher Creek wet gas field some 27 wells were drilled with big and small companies, Canadian and American, participating in the costly and lengthy hunt. But they had not yet found the oil.
In 1941-we are coming up to the great outburst which resulted in the discovery of oil and gas in a big way in Alberta-the Canadian Gulf Oil Company, a unit of the big Gulf Oil Corporation of Pittsburgh, decided to embark upon an Alberta program. One of the things at stake in this great debate now is this. Are great companies like the Gulf company of the United States to be discouraged into thinking that no matter how much money they spend in developing great projects like this, there will be simpletons in the Canadian House of Commons who will block every effort to enable them to market their goods or are we going to act in such a way as to give them confidence?
Let us go on with the story. First, Gulf Oil had one of its geologists start a preliminary reconnaissance. In 1942 Gulf Oil set its scientists to work with seismographs and gravity meters in a hunt for structures and information, following clues over 9,000 square miles in southwestern Alberta. By 1946 they had poured over $4 million into the hunt but had not probed into the earth except with shotholes of seismograph crews and shallow structure test bore holes. The company scientists, even after this high cost search, were not at all sure of success. The best prospect they had located was a deeply buried anticlinal structure or ridge south of Pincher Creek and not far from the shallow drilling of nearly half a century before. We are taking steps to show how much we need the great, powerful concerns of the United States to discover our oil.
Gulf Oil had to consider whether or not to take a very risky gamble and drill to test whether gas or oil lay below the Madison limestone formation, which is the productive core of the Turner valley field 100 miles to the north. This core would have to be reached and pierced. They knew that the Madison limestone could be anywhere from 11,000 to 14,500 feet underground. The cost of the necessary deep drill tests might be $1 million. The odds were at least 10 to 1 that the Madison might not be productive when it was penetrated, and all that money might be spent in vain.
'Mr. Blackmore.]

Gulf decided to take the gamble and in January 1947, a few weeks before Imperial Oil discovered the Leduc field, Gulf announced that it would drill its Pincher Creek No. 1 wildcat. Gulf Oil gathered itself for the challenging effort. It contracted for one of the most powerful drilling rigs then in existence, capable of cutting a hole 15,000 feet deep through hard rock, at a price of nearly $1 million. All this goes to show how helpless we would be in getting this development if we did not have powerful concerns ready to take the risk.

Why does not the hon. member show a little common sense instead of talking so much talk?
On April 23, 1947, Gulf began to drill and the battle was on. Eight months went by, months of unremitting strain for all concerned. Then the crew reached the Madison limestone at a depth of 11,700 feet, over two miles into the foothills of the rockies. Fifty-five feet into the Madison they bored and they struck porous lime, the container for oil, gas or water. If it was water, then of course all their efforts would have been in vain. They drilled 45 feet farther and halted at 11,800 feet, having set a North American record for an open hole.
The danger to the well was extreme. The pressure on a nine inch diameter hole at over two miles of depth is tremendous. Surface casing extended from the top to a point 440 feet down, but below that were 11,360 feet of hole unprotected except for the mud coating left by the drilling mud which was kept continuously circulating through the drill pipe to bring rock cuttings to the surface. In order to protect the well a seven inch casing was run and cemented to 11,755 feet.
Then on December 28, 1947, a drill stem test was run to determine the contents of the porous rock. The drill stem test proved that the field was under enormous and very dangerous pressure; second, that there was a highly gratifying deposit of wet gas. This was only the beginning, Mr. Speaker, of the tremendous story of the discovery of gas in Alberta.
Let me ask hon. members of the Conservative party at least, who do make a pretense at having sense; why run the chance of discouraging companies who would come into Alberta and Canada to find field after field like this, greatly to the blessing of the whole Dominion of Canada and perhaps the means of saving us in case of a war? Can you afford to take the chance of delaying this bill, delaying construction of this pipe

line and perhaps destroying this company, thus rendering almost impossible the buildup of another company, with great loss to this nation?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think for the time being I shall defer the remainder of this story and tell it at some future time.

I had the privilege of either sitting behind or sitting in the government of all the premiers of Saskatchewan, or sitting in opposition to them, except the present one; and I sat with the present premier in this house. The first public ownership scheme in the province of Saskatchewan was the telephone system, which was set up in 1906, the year after the province was formed. We have had government-owned, controlled and operated telephones practically all through the history of the province, set up under the Liberal government of Hon. Walter Scott.

Well, I am sure my hon. friends will agree with me when I say that practically all the profits they have ever made under government ownership and government control- socialization, so to speak-have been made from the telephones and the power commission set up by the Liberals while they were in power. "The action proposed today is another declaration of independence by Canada ..."
That is an interesting expression.
May I say we have been listening here for some days to speeches being made and terms being applied to members on both sides of the house, and I would just like to submit my opinion with regard to what really does give a person the right to rise in his place on the floor of this house and raise a question of privilege. I am quite certain that when the leader of the C.C.F. party said to my friend back here that he was representing certain corporations in this house, if there is no privilege in connection with that then there is no privilege in connection with anything.
That was a real question of privilege. No hon. member has the right to come to this house to represent here any particular corporations, or any particular individuals for that matter. He represents a constituency, and on being elected he comes here to speak for all the people in the Dominion of Canada on these different issues. If he is accused in this house by another member of being here to represent some particular corporation or industry then, of course, he has the right of privilege to bring it up, and such statements ought to be withdrawn. But I think this one

with regard to the Minister of Trade and Commerce caps them all:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is confused, you see, as to what country he is supposed to be serving.
Now, what is that based on? That is based on the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was born in the United States. He goes on to emphasize it. Well, I would like to suggest to this house that at least 25 per cent, and probably more, of all Canadians we have in this country were born in some other country and came here. I would also like to suggest that statements of this kind do no credit to this house, and certainly do no credit to those who send members here who make that kind of statement. There are a lot of people in Canada who will remember statements of that kind and see to it that some of those who make them do not come back again.

Anyone who has ever served in a federal government knows that every minister receives proposals every day, sometimes marked confidential and sometimes not marked confidential, which he does not take to council. If that were not the case we would get no business done at all.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
What is the position in connection with this particular project? Well, in the first place there are two points of importance. The first is that this line must be kept on the Canadian side of the border for certain reasons, and anyone in this house can easily determine what are those reasons. The second point is that in so far as the gas is needed in this country it must be kept on this side of the line.
If anyone wishes to determine why certain steps were taken about which questions were raised this afternoon all they need do is refer back to those two facts, both of which were basic in Sir John A.'s beliefs. After all, as was stated a few moments ago, gas was discovered in Alberta some time ago in considerable quantities. The government of Alberta quite properly said in the beginning they wanted to make absolutely certain there was going to be sufficient gas reserved within the boundaries of Alberta in order to make it possible to develop industry there and maintain it to the extent which is necessary. After further development, and after examining the available supply, they could confidently say some 500 million cubic feet per day could be exported from Alberta. That matter was, of course, discussed by the federal government, and it was discussed in relation to a pipe line.
It was suggested by some people that we build a pipe line down to Winnipeg and from there to the south, making no provision whatever for the building of a line beyond Winnipeg to the central part of Canada, and merely to allow a company to continue selling gas in the United States until they made enough money to build the line through the northern part of Ontario and on into the eastern part of Canada. Questions like that were discussed by the government, and the government came to the conclusion that this kind of thing could not be allowed to happen.
Why? In the first place, if you allowed that gas to go down across the line at Emerson into the United States and on down to Minneapolis and Chicago-it was even suggested that we try to push it around to Detroit and into eastern Canada-you would establish there private interests which would be interested in the retention of the gas in that section of the country, interests which you could not discard in future without causing a great deal of trouble with the country to the south. The government naturally decided that any system that was set up had to be on a basis which would keep a certain amount of gas for this country. The figure struck was 300 million cubic feet per day which could be used in this country and therefore had to be retained here for our use.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Of course a question arises as to what is going to happen in the future. That will depend on the further production of gas and its distribution. Before they can get any increase of gas across the border they must get a permit from this government in order to take it across. In other words it has been made absolutely certain that any gas which is required in this country is going to be kept on this side of the line and used here. Many people say it has something to do with the cost. That reminds me of some things which took place in my own province. Great boasts have been made about the fact that gas is to be taken into two of our cities under a government-owned and controlled system.

-and 84 cents in Prince Albert, and under this plan gas is going to be sold in Winnipeg for 30 cents. I am sure you will be saying a great deal about that if you decide to reside permanently in Regina. That is something that is happening under government ownership and control, and about which our friends do not tell us the whole story.
Provision is being made under this system to keep gas on this side of the line, and to build only an arm of the line to take out whatever surplus gas there is, which we are sure we can allow to go into the United States without interfering with conditions here and without creating vested interests on the other side of the line which we cannot maintain. All that is protected by this scheme.
Let me ask you this question. When Mr. McMahon came along and offered to do this job and said he could finance it, what were the conditions in the offer? He could finance it if we would allow him to ship 400 million cubic feet of gas per day into the United States for 25 years. That would cut us down to a supply of 100 million cubic feet per day, one-third of what we require in this country. Once having established that situation on the other side of the line, how could the government or anyone else change it?
Talk about placing control on the south side of the line. If you want to establish control over anything on this side of the line just make it possible to ship it down there and establish vested interests on the other side of the line; then try to take it away and you will find out whether or not you are under the
!Mr. Gardiner.]
United States control. It is a matter of keeping the gas here. We must not create vested interests we cannot continue to supply.
It makes no difference where the Minister of Trade and Commerce had that proposal; whether he had it in his inside coat pocket as my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert would lead us to believe, whether he put it in the safe or, for that matter, whether he put it in the fire. The minister knew when he read that proposal the government of Canada would not accept it.

Even this particular organization knew what the situation was in that regard, because they wanted to do that at an earlier stage, ship the gas to the United States, sell it as fast as possible, get the finances on account of it and then build the central section. They learned from the government long ago that was not permitted, and it is not permitted now. So the gas is being kept to the extent that we need it on this side of the line.
This particular bill proposes to assist financially on two different sections of the line that is to be built. The first is a government-owned project, as my hon. friends of the C.C.F. say it ought to be.

Are they going to vote the bill down because that is in it? Well, that is in it. It provides that the government of Canada and the government of Ontario, working hand in hand, one being Liberal and the other Conservative, are prepared to build that line across northern Ontario. If that line were not built across northern Ontario the only objective there would be in building the line from Alberta to Winnipeg, beyond providing Winnipeg with gas, would be to build a line to Emerson and on into the United States. So this bill provides for the setting up of the northern Ontario section, financed by the two governments.
Then it provides for the setting up of the next section west, the one from the Alberta boundary down to Winnipeg. In spite of what my hon. friends say, there is provision for the carrying on of the line until it connects with

the northern Ontario section. That connection will make a line from Alberta to the eastern section of Canada, where the greater part of the gas will be required in this country. The suggestion is made that we should not have agreed to loan some $80 million to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines so that it will be able to go ahead and build this year with that financial assistance. I understand they are putting some $15 million-odd into it themselves, and that the government is loaning them some $80 million, which the government gets back next March.
